in_context.text: Paul, writing from prison, makes his request to Philemon. He pleads for Onesimus and calls him "my son," because Onesimus came to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains. This sets up the appeal for Philemon to receive Onesimus back as a brother.

speaker.text: Paul, who calls himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ and "Paul the aged," writing with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon, a beloved fellow-worker of Paul, along with Apphia, Archippus, and the church that met in his house.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant who had left him. He had become a believer through Paul, and Colossians, carried on the same journey, calls him "a faithful and beloved brother."

what.text: Paul now names the person he is pleading for. "Begotten" here means Paul led Onesimus to faith, in the same way Paul says he "begotten" the Corinthians "through the gospel." The plea that follows is to receive him "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved."

events.text: Onesimus came to faith while Paul was imprisoned. He was then sent back to Philemon, travelling with Tychicus, who also carried Colossians.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 60-62, during Paul's imprisonment in Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison, and the letter does not name the city; Rome is the traditional view. It was sent to Philemon's household, traditionally at Colossae, since Colossians calls Onesimus "one of you."

purpose.text: Paul chooses to plead rather than command, "for love's sake." He shows a bond with Onesimus so close that he calls him his son and "mine own bowels," meaning his very heart.

big_picture.text: Paul often calls those he brought to faith his children, such as Timothy, Titus, and the Galatians. In Christ a servant becomes a beloved brother, and Paul even offers to pay any debt Onesimus owes.

for_readers.text: New birth in Christ creates real family ties. These ties cross lines of social rank, and they call believers to welcome one another.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to call on, beseech, or entreat. The lexicon notes the same word in Philemon 9. It repeats Paul's choice to plead for love's sake instead of giving an order.
The word means a child. It is also used as a kindly address from an elder to a junior or a teacher to a disciple, as in Galatians 4:19. Paul speaks of a spiritual family tie, not a family of blood.
The word means to beget, as a father does. Paul uses "begotten" the same way in 1 Corinthians 4:15, "I have begotten you through the gospel," for bringing people to faith.

The word means a band or bond, and it is used of actual chains. The lexicon lists Philippians 1:7, 13 and Colossians 4:18 among its uses. Onesimus came to faith while Paul was literally a prisoner, which v.13 calls "the bonds of the gospel."
The name means "profitable" and was common among slaves. That explains Paul's wordplay in the next verse: once "unprofitable," but now "profitable."

takeaway.text: Paul pleads for Onesimus as his own spiritual son, born to faith in Paul's chains. The gospel had made a servant who once departed part of Paul's family, and Paul asks Philemon to see him that way too.

resolved.reason: Calls Onesimus a 'runaway servant,' but the cited sources only say he departed or had left. 'Runaway' presents the traditional fugitive-slave reading as fact.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources

resolved.reason: Says Colossians 'later' calls Onesimus a faithful and beloved brother. The sources place Colossians at the same time, carried on the same journey with Tychicus, not later.
